steps: Hearth & ember protection
Non-combustible hearth raised 2" above an adjacent combustible floor, extending 16" in front and 8" beyond each side of the opening. Ember protection to the firing side: 16" USA, 18" Canada.
Check clearances
Door edge to adjacent sidewall 15", to side mantel pillar 11 1/2"; surround brow to mantel or top facing 16"; bottom of unit to ceiling 68".
Qualify & prepare the fireplace

Masonry wood-burning fireplace, opening at least 34" W × 22" H × 20" D, chimney 15' minimum. Repair cracks or loose mortar, check the chimney for creosote or obstructions, lock the damper open or remove it.

Fireplace built to N.F.P.A. 211 (latest edition) or applicable codes; installation to CAN/CSA-B365. Never a makeshift or “temporary” installation.

  • Opening minimums: 34" (864 mm) wide, 22" (559 mm) high, 20" (508 mm) deep.
  • Chimney 15' (4.57m) minimum, suitable for wood burning. Check for creosote buildup or obstructions, especially if it hasn't been used for some time.
  • Repair cracks, loose mortar or other defects before installing.
  • Lock the existing damper open or remove it completely.
  • Don't remove bricks or mortar. Exception: masonry or steel, including the damper plate, may be removed from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit a liner, if that doesn't weaken the fireplace and chimney or reduce protection for combustibles below the National Building Code.
  • If the fireplace was modified for the insert, fasten the supplied metal tag to its back wall.
  • Designed for a flush hearth: if the hearth material is raised above the fireplace floor, put spacers under the front edge so the weight doesn't rest on the control assembly beneath the ashlip.
Note: the rating label (p. 3) says to install and use only in a “masonry or factory built fireplace”; p. 15 says “This Insert shall not be installed in a factory-built fireplace.” The label's French text says masonry fireplace only, not factory-built.
Install the liner
Full flue liner to the top of the chimney (required in Canada, recommended by Pacific Energy) or, USA only, a direct flue connection to the first flue tile. Never share a flue with another appliance.

Two flue connections are acceptable in most areas; follow local and national codes. Pacific Energy highly recommends the full liner as the safest installation with optimum performance: the insert drafts correctly, avoiding difficult start-ups and smoking out the door.

Full flue liner (required in Canada)

Listed stainless steel rigid or flexible liner from the insert flue collar to the top of the chimney. Canada: continuous 5" (127mm) to 6" (150mm) liner, Class 3 to CAN/ULC-S635 or CAN/ULC-S640. USA: flue liner conforming to UL-1777.

  1. Measure the chimney height from the top of the existing flue to the floor of the hearth (leaves extra for flashing and rain cap).
  2. Feed the liner from the top of the chimney, through the damper area, into the fireplace cavity.
  3. Attach a chimney connector to the bottom of the liner, then the removable flue collar to the connector with 3 stainless steel screws.

Direct flue connection (USA only)

  1. Measure from the first chimney flue liner to the top of the insert, allowing extra to insert into the flue tile.
  2. Feed the stainless steel liner through the damper area into the first chimney flue tile and seal around the pipe.

Local codes may require a clean-out door with a direct flue connection. Figure 6 labels the liner 6" stainless steel rigid or flex.

Don't connect this unit to a chimney flue serving another appliance.
Connect, set & level
Remove the baffle for access, push the insert in, connect the removable flue collar and level with the rear adjusting legs. Full liner: flash the top, caulk with RTV silicone, fit the rain cap.

The connector and removable flue collar are reached through the insert's flue outlet, so remove the baffle first:

  1. Remove the retaining pin at the back of the firebox, just under the baffle.
  2. Lift the baffle to disconnect it from the baffle supply tube.
  3. Pull it toward you, tilt it sideways and drop it out. If needed, remove the opposite brick rail: take out the brick under it, then lift the rail up and inward to clear the locating pins.
  4. Inspect the baffle-to-supply-tube gasket; replace if necessary (prt#80000365).

Push the insert into position. Full liner: attach the flue collar to the opening in the top of the firebox. Direct connection: attach the removable flue collar to the liner. Level with the rear adjusting legs, then reinstall the baffle in reverse order.

Full liner, chimney top: measure, trim and shape a top flashing with 1" (25mm) to 1-1/2" (38mm) overlap on each side and seat it firmly against the tile. Screw the flashing collar to the liner, caulk the gap with RTV silicone and attach a rain cap (storm collar optional).

Don't operate with the baffle assembly, tubes or insulation removed.
The full-liner section (p. 16) points to “page 8” for baffle removal; the procedure is on p. 11.
Fit the surround

Screw the backing plate to the unit's mounting brackets (four screws), push the unit back until the plate meets the fireplace facing, then hook the front trim into the slots between the fan mount brackets and the firebox, sliding it down to engage.
Combustion air

Outside air: replace the ash clean-out cover with a rodent screen, keep the air inlet uncovered, seal the back surround to the fireplace. Room air: drawn from the front under the firebox; may need make-up air.
Power & blowers
Plug the 115V, 60 Hz, 1.2 AMP blowers into a grounded three-prong outlet, cord routed away from the unit. The cord exits right as shipped; moving it left costs approximately 12" of length.

Circulating air blowers115V, 60 Hz, 1.2 AMP
Cord exitRight side, as shipped

Use only a properly grounded outlet that accepts a three-prong plug; don't cut or remove the grounding prong. Follow local codes, or CSA C22.1 (Canada) / ANSI/NFPA 70 (USA). Route the power cord away from the unit.

Moving the cord to the left side

  1. Remove the two screws securing the control assembly; disconnect the wires to the right-side blower.
  2. Remove the power cord from the slot in the right-side end of the control assembly.
  3. Remove the two screws securing the backing plate with the strain relief and rotate it 180 degrees.
  4. Engage the cord in the slot on the left-side end of the control assembly.
  5. Reconnect the right-side blower wires and reinstall the control assembly.

The cord loses approximately 12" (305mm) of length on the left side.
Firebricks
Rear wall first, then the side walls, then the floor (Figures 15–21). One full-sized “A” brick is left over as a spare.

A · 5096.999" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4"
B · 7847.32 1/8" X 9" X 1 1/4"
C · 78474 1/2" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4"
D · 7847.12 1/8" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4"
  1. Rear wall: two “A” bricks vertical behind the right-hand tab on the rear brick rail, slid toward the centre; then two “A” with one “B” between them against the left side, slid toward the centre.
  2. Side wall: three “A” vertical, pushed back to meet the rear “A” bricks; a “C” on top of an “A”.
  3. One “A” horizontal on top of the three side “A” bricks, inserted behind the tab.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 on the opposite side wall.
  5. Floor, rear: an “A” in each corner with one “B” between them.
  6. Two “A” in front of the rear left-hand corner “A”.
  7. Two “A” on the right-hand side of the floor, then the “D” in the centre in front of the “B”.

One full-sized “A” brick is left over as a spare. Firebrick set, NEO 2.5: 80000248.

panels.title: Smoke / won't burn (draft too low)
items: Back puffing, or smoke leaking at appliance and connector joints → inadequate draft
Chimney plugged or restricted → inspect and clean the flue
Improper chimney height or diameter, oversized or unsuitable chimney → consult dealer
Combustion air supply blocked → check the outside air supply for obstructions

panels.title: Too much draft / over-firing
items: Uncontrollable burn, or a glowing red stove part or chimney → excessive draft
Glowing red top or vent pipe → over-firing; can permanently damage heater and chimney
Full load on a hot coal bed with the air wide open longer than needed to char it → excessively hot fire

panels.title: Excessive creosote / dirty glass
items: Wood too wet → use dry wood (recommended moisture level below 20%)
Air turned down too soon → wait for a good bed of coals and charred wood
Draft too low → check flue, chimney height and diameter, provide outside air
Dirty glass: door gasket leakage → replace gasket, check door latch

panels.title: Low heat / won't burn overnight
items: Wood may be wet → use drier wood
Fire too small → build a larger fire, open the draft control
Won't burn overnight: air control set too high → set it lower
Not enough wood → unsplit wood is preferred for overnight burns

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
You need crumpled newspaper, dry kindling and a few small pieces of dry wood. Build the fire right on the firebricks, never on a grate or andirons.

  1. Move the air control to High (all the way to the left) and open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the firebox. Crisscross several pieces of dry kindling over it, then add a few small pieces of dry wood on top.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open about 1/2" to 1" until the kindling is fully in flames.
  4. Add a few small logs and close the door.
  5. When there's a good bed of coals and the wood has charred, set the air control for normal burning.
Never start or freshen up a fire with gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or any other chemical or volatile liquid. Keep all such liquids well away from the insert while it is in use.
Your first 2–3 fires bake the paint on. Open all windows and doors, because the smoke and fumes can bother some people. Smoke alarms may go off more often while the paint cures. Don't disconnect them.

The glass gets hot enough to burn. Keep children, clothing and furniture away, and don't touch the glass until it has cooled.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
The air control is how you set the fire. High is all the way to the left; Low is all the way to the right.

  • After lighting or adding wood, keep the air fairly wide open, especially for the first 10 to 30 minutes, when most of the smoke is made. After about 30 minutes you can turn it down a lot without much smoke.
  • Find your setting by trial and error. Every home's heating needs differ, and the type of wood, outside temperature and weather all change the right setting. Note what works for next time.
  • Smoke pouring down across the glass (a “waterfall”) means you turned the air down too soon or too low.
  • High “H” gives the maximum firing rate. Use it only for starting a fire or preheating a fresh load.
Don't over-fire. A glowing red top or vent pipe means the fire is too hot. Over-firing can permanently damage the insert and chimney, and may void the warranty.

The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory, and altering it is against federal regulations. Tampering with the air control assembly voids the warranty and can be very hazardous.

reload.title: Reloading & overnight burns
reload.html:
Adding wood

  1. Move the air control to High and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. This stops smoke puffing back into the room.
  3. Load wood parallel to the front of the insert, with gaps so air can flow between the logs. Mix shapes and sizes, up to 18" long. Always use dry wood.
  4. Don't load wood so high, or in such a way, that opening the door becomes hazardous.

Smaller loads burn cleaner: two or three logs at a time, or 1/4 to 1/2 of a full load. Don't turn the air down too quickly after loading.

Overnight burns

Unsplit logs work best. Char the wood completely on the maximum setting before you turn the air down. Never try to burn overnight with green or wet wood.

Restarting from embers

  1. Open the door and rake the hot embers toward the front. Add a couple of dry, split logs on top and close the door.
  2. Set the air control to High. The logs should start burning within a few minutes.
  3. Once the wood has charred, set the air control where you want it.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only, air-dried (seasoned) for six months or more. Seasoned hardwoods give higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwoods or green wood. Store wood under cover, away from open flame or heat.

Wet wood smoulders, makes heavy smoke and creosote, gives little heat (up to 25% less output) and tends to go out. Aim for moisture below 20%.

Quick dryness test

Put a large piece on a good, big bed of coals:

  • Dry: it's burning on more than one side within one minute.
  • Damp: it turns black and lights within three minutes.
  • Too wet: it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes. Don't burn it.

Never burn

Wet, green or unseasoned wood, treated wood, salt water wood, garbage, coal or charcoal, cardboard, paper products, plywood or particleboard, lawn clippings or yard waste, railroad ties, anything containing plastic, rubber (tires included) or asbestos, paints, paint thinners, solvents, waste petroleum products or asphalt products, construction or demolition debris, manure and animal remains, or flammable fluids such as gasoline, naphtha or engine oil. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the insert ineffective and cause smoke. Never barbecue in the insert: other fuels, such as charcoal, can produce large amounts of carbon monoxide, a tasteless, odourless gas that can kill.

Note: The do-not-burn list (p. 6) includes wet, green and unseasoned wood, and p. 7 says to burn wood only, dry and well seasoned. p. 7 also says that if you feel it is necessary to burn wet or unseasoned wood, do so only with the air inlet set open enough to maintain a good strong fire and fairly high chimney temperatures, and not to attempt an overnight burn with green or wet wood. Wet wood can cause up to a 25% drop in heater output and adds significantly to creosote buildup.
Salt water wood and garbage contain chlorides that rapidly destroy metal and void the warranty. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Glass darkens with slow fires or poor wood. Clean it with fireplace glass cleaner, and only when the insert is cold.

  • Never scrape with anything that could scratch the glass, and don't use abrasive cleaners.
  • Don't slam the door. Make sure no logs stick out far enough to hit the glass when you close it.

What the deposit tells you

A light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily usually means good combustion, dry wood, and fairly clean pipes and chimney. A black, greasy film that's hard to remove comes from wet or green wood and burning too slowly, and it's building up in your chimney at least as fast.

Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the insert again. Use only 18" x 10-1/4" x 5 mm ceramic glass from your dealer. Don't substitute any other type.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Only remove ashes when the insert is cold.

  • Take out the excess when the ash is 3" to 4" deep and the fire has burned down and cooled.
  • Leave about 1" of ash on the firebox bottom. It helps keep a hot charcoal bed.
  • Keep the front of the firebox clear of heavy ash buildup. That's where boost combustion air comes in, and too much ash blocks it.

Safe disposal

Put ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you'll bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have cooled completely. Don't put any other waste in that container.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire. Some creosote is unavoidable; regular inspection and cleaning is the answer.

  • Inspect the chimney and connector at least once every two months during the heating season. Remove creosote once it reaches 3 mm or more.
  • Until you learn your pattern, check for creosote daily. Weekly cleaning may be needed in mild weather; monthly is usually enough in the coldest months.
  • Dry wood and plenty of air on fresh loads keep creosote down.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If it happens: get everyone ready to leave and meet outside. Close the air control. Call the fire department and keep an extinguisher handy. Don't light another fire until the chimney has been cleaned and checked for stress and cracks, and nearby combustibles and the roof have been checked.

A certified installer or chimney sweep, such as one from the National Fireplace Institute (NFI) or the Chimney Safety Institute of America (CSIA), is strongly recommended to inspect and service your chimney.

care.title: Weekly & monthly checks
care.html:
Check these parts for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections and bad warping.

Weekly

  • Firebricks: look for cracks. Replace broken or missing bricks.
  • Door gasket: sagging, out of place or damaged.

Monthly

  • Brick rails and their tabs
  • Air riser tube at the back of the firebox
  • Back side of the airwash chamber
  • Baffle locking pin
  • Boost tube cover holes, at the bottom front of the firebox

Some baffle warping, up to 1/4", is normal. Replace the baffle if it's warped more than that, cracked or broken. Never run the insert with the baffle, tubes or insulation removed.

The door gasket needs only light pressure to seal, which helps it last. Replacement gasket kits are available from your Pacific Energy dealer.
Call your dealer if you find damage. Running the insert with broken parts can speed up damage to other parts and may void your warranty.

blower.title: Using the blowers
blower.html:
Your insert comes equipped with variable-speed circulating air blowers. They have two modes, chosen with the rocker switch, and a speed control sets how fast they run.

  • Automatic: push the rocker switch to “O” (Auto) and pick a speed. The blowers turn on once the insert reaches operating temperature, and off after the fire is out and it has cooled. On and off times vary with each installation.
  • Manual: push the rocker switch to “l” (Manual) and pick a speed. This bypasses the temperature switch, so you have full control.

Suggested speeds

With the air control on Low (all the way to the right), run the blowers on Low. With the air control above Low, use whatever speed you like.

Cleaning

At least every six months, vacuum the grill openings at the back and bottom of the blower casing to remove dust and debris. Disconnect power before servicing.

The maintenance checks on p. 10 call them “the optional blowers”; the Blowers section on p. 19 says the insert comes equipped with them, and the maker's website lists the blowers under Standard Features.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy's Limited Lifetime Wood Products Warranty covers the original registered purchaser.

Limited lifetime (10 years), parts onlyPorcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage only, not impact), plating, firebox, baffle
3 years, parts and laborAny defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches
Not in lifetime coverageFirebox rails, heat shields
Not warrantedFirebrick, gaskets, ceramic fiber blankets

What can void it

  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification
  • Excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel (high sodium content, plastics or chemicals)
  • Tampering with the air control; over-firing or running with broken parts may also void it

Labor isn't covered under the lifetime part. For service, give your Pacific Energy dealer proof of purchase, the purchase date, and the model name and serial number. The serial number is on the certification label (bottom back corner of the side casing, door-catch side) and on the cover of your installation manual. You can register the product at pacificenergy.net/register.

The label's French text on p. 3 reads masonry only / not prefabricated, matching p. 15. Also flagged in the step 'Qualify & prepare the fireplace'.

Both are shown, with a sentence saying so.

review.notes: Single Installation & Operation Manual (28 pages, English; the rating label on p. 3 is bilingual and only its English text was used, except that the factory-built note also reports the label's French wording, masonry fireplace only, which agrees with p. 15). Wood insert lit by hand: no ignition system, remote or code table, so codes is empty. Not stated anywhere in the manual, so those catalog values are unchecked: weight, firebox volume, heating area, glass viewing area, blower cfm, maximum cordwood output, combustion type and stainless baffle/tube material. Figure-only content not transcribed: overall unit dimensions and surround sizes (Figure 1 p. 12, options drawing p. 26), an unlabeled 26 1/2 in dimension in Figure 2 (p. 12), the 17 1/8 in USA / 19 1/8 in Canada dimensions in Figure 3 (p. 13), and the firebrick positions beyond what the step text says (Figures 15-21). The Figure 4 callout 'mantel distance measured from hearth' and the Figure 6 liner label were used because their text is unambiguous. The full-liner section (p. 16) refers to 'Baffle Removal section page 8'; the procedure is on p. 11 (p. 17 cites p. 11 correctly). Metric equivalents for the same inch clearances differ slightly between the label (p. 3), the p. 14 table and Figure 4 (e.g. 11 1/2 in as 295, 290 and 292 mm); the guide shows inches only for clearances. The warranty heading reads 'LTD Lifetime Coverage (10 years)' and is shown as printed. The p. 3 rating statement cites 'ASTM 3053' while the label reads 'ASTM E3053'. Rocker switch positions are shown as printed ('O' auto, 'l' manual). The catalog's US availability is marked unclear; the manual says only 'certified for use in Canada and U.S.A.'. Website notes (Oct 12): specOutput quotes Heat Output (Cord Wood) 85,000 BTU from website.json and '60,000 BTU EPA Test Fuel' from the maker's live product page (Technical Data), a row website.json omits. The page prints no EPA output range, so the catalog's 15800 / 59900 have no website note. specFuel quotes Log Size (Recommended) 16". The website's firebox size, glass viewing area, weight and blower cfm aren't in the manual and are not shown.
